title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
This is a records and disclosure failure in the aftermath of a fatal crash involving a driver-assistance system, not a failure of the driving software alone. According to the reporting, the vehicle's stored data showed that the system detected a hazard before the crash, and the company told the family of the deceased that the data was gone. A hacker later recovered it, contradicting the claim that it was missing.

The failure sits in the evidence chain after deployment, in what a manufacturer retains, reports and hands over when its system is involved in a death. Catching it would not have required better sensors or a better driving policy. It would have required independent access to the vehicle's own logs, or verification of the company's account rather than acceptance of it. The court record includes orders on summary judgment and on a motion to set the verdict aside, and a jury award of more than $240 million that a judge upheld at $243 million.

What is not established here is the substance of the underlying reporting. The summary supplied with this incident is not a readable account of it, so the sequence of the crash, the state of the system at the moment of impact and any question of intent are not set out. A civil verdict upheld on review is a finding of liability, not proof of intent.
